children: By Martin Baccardax

The European Central Bank kicked-off a crucial stretch of key policy from major economies around the world Thursday with a well-telegraphed lift of its key lending rate tied to inflation stemming from the U.S. war with Iran.
Just don't expect the Federal Reserve to immediately follow suit.

Four of the world's biggest central banks are primed to either boost their key lending rates, or signal tighter policy ahead, over the next eight days, with the ECB starting things off this week with a quarter point rate hike that takes its deposit rate to 2.5%.

"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures [and] the outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside for inflation and to the downside for economic growth," the ECB said.

The Fed's September rate decision next Wednesday, of course, will be the biggest of the bunch, and will be paired with a fresh set of growth, inflation, and job market forecasts that will peer into conditions expected in 2029.

Investors looking for direction from the ECB, however, as the Fed recalibrates its communications policy under new Chairman Kevin Warsh and eyes oil and bond market dynamics into the end of the year, could be disappointed.
Thursday's larger event, at least in Fed terms, came from an in-line reading of factory gate inflation, parts of which feed into the Fed's preferred rate-setting metric, the core PCE price index.

Friday's release of consumer price inflation data for August is also likely to prove crucial, but investors are expecting little change from core readings, which strip out volatile components like energy prices.

None of that, of course, factors in the massive surge in oil prices witnessed over the past two months, tied to the U.S. war with Iran, which have added more than 40% to Brent crude prices and taken them firmly north of the $100 mark.
Major increases in gas prices, which are now 34% higher than last year's levels at $4.26 a gallon, and diesel fuel, now trading at a record high of just under $6 a gallon, have followed suit.

But, as ING's global head of Macro Carsten Brzeski notes, the market's biggest concern at present is how the Fed, and central banks around the world, navigate their key challenge: inflation or overtightening risk.
Should oil prices fade quickly on a Gulf war resolution, or even a tamp down in the recent tit-for-tat hostilities, headline inflation pressures will retreat in kind.
But higher rates would choke off growth, and crowd out investment, at the same time.

On the flip side, faster oil and energy price increases will have knock-on effects to the broader economy, in the form of gas, diesel, and potentially wage pressures, that could spiral quickly if left unchecked by the Fed.
Bond markets are already suggesting that risk.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield, perhaps the most important interest rate in the world, is trading at around 4.92%, the highest since 2023, while the longer-dated 30-year bond yield hit a fresh 2007 high of 5.35%.

And those moves, which have added around 55 basis points to 10-year yields over the past two months alone, have come despite renewed intervention efforts from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and a plan to prevent Japan from selling U.S. government bonds to support its volatile currency.

"The Treasury Secretary has been rather confident in his ability to steer markets the way he wants them to go, but it doesn't seem to be working so far," said Kent Fung, vice president for market intelligence at Fundstrat.
Will Warsh, who has adopted a far less bellicose approach, have more luck in bringing markets closer to a Fed rate vision that he's loath to articulate?
He has some work to do.
The CME Group's FedWatch tool pegs the probability of a Fed rate hike next week at around 70%, a high enough number to suggest markets have come to an early decision.
Stocks are trading heavily, as well, with the S&P 500 down around 2.5% from the all-time high it reached in mid-August, and drifting further into negative territory for the month.
But what can't be ignored at the same time is political pressure, which came last week in the form of a missive from President Donald Trump following a surprising solid August jobs report.
"Lower the rate or I'll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit", the president said, adding that "The Fed Board, with its great new leader must get smart-BE Patriots for a change."

Warsh, put in place by Trump a few months ago under the explicit pretense that he would keep interest rates low, will be mindful of the optics of hiking two months before midterm elections. He may also opt to work on reducing the Fed's bloated balance sheet.

Or he might conclude that bond markets are reacting as much to growth and deficit figures, both of which are well beyond the Fed's remit, as they are to inflation pressures and possible Fed policy changes.

The market's biggest question now, it seems, is whether Warsh will defy his new boss, less than 50 days out from the November elections, or cede to the markets which he brashly lectured earlier this summer to think for themselves.
Both options are less than ideal, and could challenge Fed credibility early in Warsh's new term.

"Our issue is not the hope that getting inflation down will be done with minimal pain, but with conveying the impression that this outcome can be counted on," said Steve Englander, who heads global G-10 FX research at Standard Chartered.
We'll know more next week, but markets have already spoken loudly.
